why: Allotropes of an element are its different crystalline forms, so every allotrope of carbon must be made of carbon atoms only. Section 9.6.1 lists the allotropes of carbon the chapter teaches: diamond (each carbon bonded tetrahedrally to four others through \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybrid orbitals), graphite (two-dimensional sheets of \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) carbons), fullerene (\(\mathrm{C_{60}}\), described in the same section as the soccer-ball-shaped Buckminsterfullerene or **bucky ball**), carbon nanotubes and graphene. So bucky ball, diamond and graphite are all allotropes of carbon and each is ruled out. Emerald is not a form of carbon at all — it is a gemstone variety of the mineral beryl, a beryllium aluminium silicate — and it is named nowhere in the chapter's list of carbon allotropes. Emerald is therefore the odd one out.

The chapter states this fact directly in the 'Do you know ?' box beside section 9.4.3: *Boron nitride is also called inorganic graphite.* The name is earned because boron nitride crystallises in sheets of fused six-membered B-N rings that stack exactly the way graphite's hexagonal carbon sheets do, B and N together supplying the same number of valence electrons as two carbon atoms. Each of the other three is a boron compound the chapter treats elsewhere and none is layered like graphite: borax, \(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7 \cdot 10H_2O}\), is the white crystalline salt of section 9.8.1; diborane, \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\), is the electron-deficient hydride of section 9.7.4 held together by banana bonds; and colemanite is the calcium borate mineral \(\mathrm{Ca_2B_6O_{11}}\) from which section 9.8.1 prepares borax.

Section 9.8.3 names Haber's process explicitly under the preparation of ammonia: on the large scale ammonia is prepared by direct combination of dinitrogen and dihydrogen, \(\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)}\), at about \(200 \times 10^5\) Pa and \(\sim 700\) K over an iron-oxide catalyst promoted with \(\mathrm{K_2O}\) and \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\). So the product of Haber's process is ammonia. The others are each made by a different route the chapter does not attribute to Haber: nitric acid \(\mathrm{(HNO_3)}\) is listed in section 9.8.3 among the compounds *manufactured from* ammonia rather than by this process; urea \(\mathrm{(NH_2CONH_2)}\) is likewise named there as a fertiliser made from ammonia, and section 9.8.3 in fact runs the reaction the other way, decomposing urea to give ammonia; and \(\mathrm{NH_4OH}\) is simply the aqueous solution formed when the ammonia has already been made and is dissolved in water.

Thallium is the heaviest member of group 13, whose group oxidation state is \(+3\). The 'Remember' box in section 9.4.1 explains that in heavier p-block elements the oxidation state lowered by two units from the group value becomes increasingly stable because of the **inert pair effect** — the two valence s-electrons are shielded poorly by the ten inner d-electrons, are held more tightly, and so take part less readily in bonding. Thallium therefore shows both \(+3\) and \(+1\), with \(+1\) the more stable, exactly as the worked example on \(\mathrm{Tl^{\oplus 1}}\) versus \(\mathrm{Tl^{\oplus 3}}\) concludes. The other options fail on the facts: thallium is not an inner transition element, it is a p-block element of group 13; being a metal cannot be the reason, since metallic character is shared by In, Ga and Al without producing a comparably stable \(+1\) state; and Table 9.2 gives thallium an electronegativity of only 1.8, so it is not highly electronegative.

All four options are group 14 elements, so the question is which of them shows the inert pair effect most strongly. Section 9.4.1 states that the lower oxidation state becomes increasingly stable *as we move down to heavier elements in the groups*, and the 'Remember' box attributes this to the poor shielding of the valence s-electrons by the ten inner d-electrons — an effect that only appears once those d-electrons are present and that grows with the number of intervening inner shells. Ordering the four by position in group 14 gives C (period 2), Si (period 3), Ge (period 4) and Pb (period 6), so lead is the heaviest and shows the effect most prominently. Carbon and silicon lie above the first d-block series and have no inner d-electrons to weaken the shielding at all, so neither shows the effect; germanium does, but lies two periods above lead, and the worked example on \(\mathrm{GeCl_4}\) and \(\mathrm{PbCl_2}\) settles the comparison directly by concluding that the stability of the \(+2\) state is greater in Pb than in Ge.
